Objective for processing:  
Osteoarthritis (OA) is a musculoskeletal chronic condition, albeit not age related, tends to be highly prevalent in the population over 40 years old, fairly increasing in acuteness of symptoms overtime; ultimately leading to decreased physical mobility, joint stiffness and acute pain. Joint pain is commonly understood as an age related phenomena, which decreases the individual likeness of seeking medical help in earlier stages of chronic OA.
As a relatively well known condition, with an established and low risk procedure, the Queen Mary University of London's (QMUL) interest in joint replacements due to OA is to evaluate the coverage of health systems that are based on equity and free-at-the-point-of-delivery care.
This research is a cross-sectional, comparative and ecologic mixed methods study; has the aims of calculating age and sex standardised hip arthroplasty rates per 100,000 people in England, Brazil and Scotland, divided by country and geographic regions for the period of 1993/94-2012/13; and analyse geographic differences from an equity perspective using quantitative and qualitative methods.
Objectives: 
1.	To compare age and sex standardised rates of hip replacements between England, Brazil and Scotland in the public sector by country and region for the period 1993/94-2012/13;
2.	To examine whether there is a socioeconomic gradient in hip arthroplasty treatment rates; 
3.	To develop a framework exploring the contribution of resource allocation health services availability (physicians and beds including public and private sectors) to differences in treatment rates; 
4.	To describe the policies with respect to technology assessment  in the  public sector of Brazil and Scotland by undertaking a documentary analysis and qualitative interviews with civil servants, policy makers and health professionals.

This research is part of a PhD study and QMUL will aim to produce articles that will be submitted to peer review journals, as recommendations to the Brazilian government regarding access to care for acute stages of osteoarthritis. This research could potentially be used to identify better allocation of resources to reduce inequality of care.
This data will not be shared with any other partners, only QMUL research staff and only used for the research outlined above.
The obtained data will not be linked with any other data. QMUL will only produce standardised rates of treatment from the data obtained from this agreement.
Processing activities: 
The data provided will be used in comparison with data from Brazil (already obtained) and NHS Scotland (already obtained), comparing access to hip replacements by age group and gender in these three countries - the data will be transformed in rates and standardised to allow comparison. The analysis will show, together with QMUL’s systematic review, the need for planning care pathways for Osteoarthritis (mainly in Brazil, where there is none) in face of the ageing population.
The data will not be used for commercial purposes by QMUL.
The data sent to Brazil and any other location will not be used for commercial purposes.
Specific outputs expected, including target date: 
By the end of this research project the results will be presented to some key persons within the Ministry of Health of Brazil, alongside the publication in international peer review journals. A diffusion of results seminar will be organised and funded by the Brazilian participants of our project, which will have a printed version with key findings. 

The publication will use just the aggregate totals, which will be standardised using census data. No patient level data will be used for the publication. 
A report will be published on QMUL website and applicant’s website www.allysonpollock.com; this report will be sent to the NIHR, PHE, HSCIC  and NHS England and Health Select committees and other policy makers including CCGs and Health and Well being Boards.
Peer review papers will be published that will be read by clinicians surgeons and clinical directors.  We have past experience of this see publication by Kirkwood Pollock et al and report to the CSO Scotland.  
Results will be communicated to the Scottish and English Hip arthroplasty projects and to the media and public at large.
Expected measurable benefits to health and/or social care including target date: 
The work will benefit the NHS in relation to planning better offer of elective care, in this specific case, elective hip arthroplasties, mainly due to Osteoarthritis. An analysis by age group will be used to compare with similar data from NHS Scotland, revealing differences in access to care. It is aimed to constructively discuss health access policies within the public health service.
The benefit of this analysis for the UK is to highlight the issues regarding an ageing population, mainly policies which focus on non-life-threatening chronic diseases and which have, however, a great impact on the quality of life of individuals - such as Osteoarthritis. The results of this research will be disseminated in health research events and publications within the UK, contributing to the scientific debate of care in osteoarthritis. 
This study will look at trends in use and area based differences and socioeconomic and age adjusted differences in access and use of services by LA area , PCT area and CCG in England.  It will replicate earlier studies by Judge in include and by Kirkwood, Pollock et al in Scotland.   It will look at differences between Scotland and England in access which will help to identify research areas which will enable QMUL to understand differences in the operation of the health systems on both sides of the border and those groups of patients who are vulnerable to not receive the care they need in England. For example, QMUL’s previous research showed that Scotland was able to reduce inequalities in access and clear waiting times without needing to resort to the private sector. It will inform the Duty as to reducing inequalities in part and more work will be required as a result of the findings.
This work will also inform the general duties of the need to promote the effective, efficient and economic use of resources in the provision of health services and of adult social care in England.  If there are geographic inequalities and socioeconomic inequalities in utilisation rates then this suggests that that the NHS is not working for patient benefit and more research is needed to understand why not.
